comments.author: djoldman
comments.text:
These proofs really are quite huge. The proof is 1.3GB, ~15M lines of code:
mkdir -p riemann_proof && cd riemann_proof
# fetch parts 01–14
for i in {01..14}; do
curl -fSL -o lean.tar.gz.part$i https://alpo.ge/lean.tar.gz.part$i || { echo "failed: part$i"; break; }
done
# join and decompress (creates ./lean)
cat lean.tar.gz.part{01..14} > lean.tar.gz
tar xzf lean.tar.gz
# size, file count, line counts
du -sh lean | cut -f1 | xargs printf '%s on disk (lean folder)\n'
find lean -name '*.lean' | wc -l | xargs printf '%s .lean files\n'
find lean -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 cat | wc -l | xargs printf '%s lines total\n'
find lean -name '*.lean' -print0 | xargs -0 cat | grep -cv '^[[:space:]]*$' | xargs printf '%s non-blank lines\n'

comments.author: dawdler-purge
comments.text:
I was  when saw this in the morning. I thought I could no longer be surprised by AI progress. Yet I had not truly believed that Claude could prove a conjecture as challenging as the Riemann Hypothesis.
In fact, just this summer, I tried to write a short science fiction story, The Last Conjecture, about AI working on the Riemann Hypothesis — a bad, unpublished story that I wrote with the help of AI itself. The irony is that even the AI helping me write it could not believe that AI would solve the Riemann Hypothesis in any near future. In its own forecast for the story, the project drags on for nine years, all the way to 2035, and still never cracks it.
Just yesterday, on Friday, I was still telling students: “Maybe there is some physical law that limits how much intelligence one can get from current LLM architectures. Surely nothing in this universe is infinite.” Maybe I am right. It is just that on November 21, 2026, we have not yet reached that limit.
It was 7 a.m. I opened the curtains in my study. The sun was rising. It was a sunny day. Nothing had changed. Everything had changed.
Seeking some solace, I listened to a recent episode of the 3Blue1Brown podcast with host Grant Sand

comments.author: chriddyp
comments.text:
Very, very excited about models of this size. Small enough to run on a Mac Mini!
Ran my 43 question data analytics exam on it against OpenRouter & my M4 Pro 64GB Mac Mini via llama. It scored a "B" on the exam [1], same score as DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Sonnet 5.
The main limitation that I saw was a "runaway loop" when asked to find a issues in a dataset: it worked for over 3 hours on my Mac Mini, taking over 180 tool calls to answer the question before I cut it off.
It's the most accurate U.S. open weight model that fits on a Mac mini that I've tested (other two are Muse Glimmer 30B and Gemma 4 31B). Against other models its size, the only model that got a better score was Qwen 3.8 27B(it got a B+).
On my Mac Mini, each question takes between 4min-30min to answer. On OpenRouter, the median was ~70s. So ~4x slower on desktop software. That should get faster when mlx support comes available.
For memory usage, Llama was taking about 29GB on my Mac Mini.
Very exciting overall!

https://plotly.com/blog/inkling-2-mini-plotly-data-analytics...

comments.author: whycombinetor
comments.text:
Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket.
From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

comments.author: nixpulvis
comments.text:
I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision.
More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams.
Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.

comments.text:
> Every node carries a backward pointer
Curious. Skiplists don't need back pointers. You can traverse a skiplist backward almost as fast as forward if you keep the "finger" around. The finger is the set of nodes from level-n down to level-0 that point as close to the goal node as possible without going beyond it. The ideal place to keep these nodes is on the stack. To traverse backwards, you do a conventional search for the starting node but every time you go down a pointer level, you push the last pointer on the stack first. Then back traversal becomes stack pops together with appropriate forward recursive calls when you pop back to a pointer that was too far to the left.
It's easier to convey the idea with code than english but I'm not typing the algorithm with my thumbs into my phone.

I think when people set out to create a chess playing computer they thought we’d end up with something that we could deeply understand at an intuitive level. Instead, when you look at the Stockfish evaluation of a position, you do get an “explanation” but it’s really just the aggregate of a bunch of calculations, which are themselves stacked on top of the “stochastic parrot” NNUE evaluator.
This leaves us in a very unsatisfying position as creatures who want answers to “why” questions. Intuitive answers are incomplete, and complete answers are either fundamentally impossible or completely incomprehensible or both.
Feynman said something similar with regards to magnetism, but I feel that understanding a chess position is an even better example. Magnetism depends on facts about the universe which at their most basic level “just are”, whereas even a complex chess position is theoretically entirely explainable.
